title: Composite types, constructors and nested mutability
outcome: Use owned types to represent data contracts and distinguish immutable bindings from recursively immutable state.
key_terms: An immutable composite type whose fields cannot be reassigned after construction.
A constructor defined inside the type body that calls `new` and can reject invalid field values before any instance exists.
A composite type whose fields can be reassigned after construction, so validation at construction alone no longer protects it.
A condition that every valid instance must satisfy, such as a finite value with a declared unit.
A mutable object, such as a vector, stored in a field of an immutable struct that can still change in place.
approach: `Measurement` has an inner constructor that converts the value with `Float64`, requires it to be finite and requires the unit to be `:m` or `:cm` before calling `new`. The struct is immutable, but `VectorRecord` stores a mutable `Vector{Int}`, so a fixed field binding can still expose changing contents.

exercises.title: Validate a unit
exercises.task: Attempt to construct a measurement with an unsupported unit.
exercises.hint: Check the invariant before new creates the object.
exercises.answer: Field types alone cannot distinguish supported and unsupported physical units.
exercises.why: `unit in (:m, :cm)` fails for anything else, so construction throws `ArgumentError` and no invalid object ever exists.
exercises.wrong: Validating units later in each analysis function lets an object with `:unknown` circulate and depends on every caller remembering the check.
exercises.verify: Example A asserts `@test_throws ArgumentError Measurement(1, :unknown)`; try `:km` as well and expect the same error.

exercises.title: Inspect conversion
exercises.answer: The conversion is deliberate and can have precision consequences for other numeric inputs.
exercises.why: The constructor calls `Float64(value)` before storing, so `Measurement(1, :cm).value` is the float 1.0.
exercises.wrong: Assuming the integer type is kept would predict `Int` storage, but `fieldtypes(Measurement)` fixes the field as `Float64`.

exercises.title: Try field reassignment
exercises.task: Reassign a field of an immutable measurement.
exercises.hint: The struct field binding is fixed after construction.
exercises.answer: This says nothing about whether the original measurement was scientifically valid.
exercises.why: Fields of an immutable struct cannot be reassigned after construction, so `measurement.value = 3.0` throws `ErrorException`.
exercises.wrong: Concluding that the failed assignment proves the measurement is valid confuses a language rule about mutation with domain validation.

exercises.title: Mutate nested storage
exercises.expected: Its contents can change despite the immutable outer struct.
exercises.answer: Deep immutability requires more than an immutable wrapper.
exercises.why: `VectorRecord(a)` stores the same vector object `a`, so `a[1] = 3` is visible as `record.values[1] == 3`.
exercises.wrong: Calling the outer struct immutable and therefore frozen predicts the old value, ignoring that the vector inside is shared and mutable.
exercises.verify: The reference performs exactly this mutation and asserts `record.values[1] == 3`.

exercises.title: Create a snapshot
exercises.task: Copy the vector before storing it in another record.
exercises.expected: Later source-vector mutation does not affect that copied vector.
exercises.hint: Choose the required storage independence explicitly.
exercises.answer: A snapshot policy must account for every nested mutable layer.
exercises.why: `VectorRecord(copy(a))` stores a fresh vector, so later writes to `a` do not reach the stored copy.
exercises.wrong: Copying the record wrapper instead of the vector still shares the inner storage, so the supposed snapshot keeps changing.
exercises.verify: The reference sets `a[1] = 4` after the copy and asserts `separate.values[1] == 3`.

exercises.title: Review a convenience constructor
exercises.task: Add a constructor with a default unit in an owned copy.
exercises.expected: It preserves the same validation contract.
exercises.hint: Route convenience paths through validated construction.
exercises.answer: An API becomes inconsistent if one creation path bypasses its stated invariant.
exercises.why: A convenience method such as `Measurement(value) = Measurement(value, :m)` routes through the inner constructor and keeps both checks.
exercises.wrong: Writing it with `new` directly or with a different field order can create objects that skip the unit and finiteness guards.
exercises.verify: Call the convenience method with NaN and expect `ArgumentError`, proving the same contract applies.

checks_note: Construction checks confirm that `Measurement` stores a `Float64` and a `Symbol`, converting the integer 1 but refusing the string "1" with `MethodError`. The vector lines show what immutability does not protect: `VectorRecord(a)` keeps a reference to `a`, so setting `a[1] = 3` is visible through `record.values`. Passing `copy(a)` breaks that link, and the later write of 4 leaves `separate.values[1]` at 3.
